voices.text: Whoever, then, thinks that he understands the Holy Scriptures, or any part of them, but puts such an interpretation upon them as does not tend to build up this twofold love of God and our neighbour, does not yet understand them as he ought.
voices.source: On Christian Doctrine 1.36.40 (trans. J. F. Shaw)

voices.text: If a reading of Scripture gives you a Father who is unlike the Son, your reading is incorrect. Scripture bears witness to the Word; it is not the Word himself (John 5:39–40). Jesus is the measure that measures all.

views.name: Historical-grammatical method
views.who: Mainstream evangelical scholarship (Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart; Grant Osborne, *The Hermeneutical Spiral*, 1991)
views.summary: Find the meaning the human author intended for the first audience, using grammar, history and genre. Then apply that meaning carefully to today.
views.strengths: Disciplined and testable. Guards against reading our ideas into the text. Respects the human authors.
views.critiques: Can stop at ‘what it meant’ and never reach Christ or the Spirit. The New Testament writers themselves read the Old Testament in ways that go beyond the human author’s intent.

views.name: Theological interpretation of Scripture
views.who: Kevin Vanhoozer; Daniel Treier; Stephen Fowl; drawing on the church fathers
views.summary: Read the Bible as Christian Scripture, within the creeds and the church’s worship, aiming to know God, not only past history.
views.strengths: Recovers the church’s long tradition of reading. Keeps Christ and the Trinity at the centre.
views.critiques: Some historians worry it lets doctrine overrule the text. Its methods can be less clearly defined.

views.name: Christ-centred and Christotelic reading
views.who: Peter Enns; Greg Boyd; Brad Jersak; Brian Zahnd; Tommy Miller; in other forms Graeme Goldsworthy and Tim Keller
views.summary: Christ is the goal (Greek *telos*) and lens of all Scripture. Every text is read in its context and then in light of Jesus, the exact image of the Father.
views.strengths: Follows the pattern of Luke 24:27 and John 5:39. Gives a clear centre for weighing hard texts.
views.critiques: Different holders mean different things by it: for Goldsworthy and Keller it confirms the whole Old Testament, while for Boyd and Jersak it reinterprets parts of it. Critics ask who defines ‘Christlike’.

views.name: Catholic and Orthodox: Scripture within Tradition
views.who: *Dei Verbum* (1965); Pontifical Biblical Commission, *The Interpretation of the Bible in the Church* (1993); Orthodox writers such as Georges Florovsky
views.summary: The Bible is the Church’s book. It is read with the Fathers, the liturgy and the teaching Church, which guards against private misinterpretation.
views.strengths: Gives a strong safeguard against individualism and a deep well of past readings.
views.critiques: Protestants ask how Scripture can correct the Church if the Church is its final interpreter.

views.name: Pentecostal and charismatic reading
views.who: Kenneth Archer (*A Pentecostal Hermeneutic*, 2004); Craig Keener (*Spirit Hermeneutics*, 2016)
views.summary: The Spirit who inspired Scripture still speaks through it. Reading is a conversation between Word, Spirit and community, expecting God to act as he did in the text.
views.strengths: Recovers expectancy and the experience of God in reading. Keener insists it must include careful historical study.
views.critiques: Without discipline, ‘the Spirit told me’ can override the text. Its best practitioners agree and tie the Spirit to Christ and Scripture.

misreadings.topic: “A good method guarantees the right answer.”
misreadings.popular: Some readers hope that if they follow the right steps, every difficult text will resolve and every disagreement end.
misreadings.inContext: Even the apostles had to work things out together (Acts 15), and Peter found some of Paul hard (2 Pet 3:16). A method makes us more honest and more humble; it does not remove all mystery (1 Cor 13:12).
misreadings.defence: Scholars of every tradition agree that methods are tools, not guarantees. Evangelicals stress that Scripture is clear on what is necessary for salvation; Catholics and Orthodox add the Church’s guidance; Pentecostals add the Spirit. None claims a method removes the need for faith and humility.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Expecting a formula can make us proud when we think we have it right, and despairing when we cannot resolve a text. The goal is faithfulness, not control.

misreadings.topic: “The Spirit step means I can skip the study steps.”
misreadings.popular: Some believers think that if the Spirit speaks to them, history, language and context do not matter.
misreadings.inContext: The same Spirit inspired the text in its original context. The Bereans received the word eagerly and also searched the Scriptures daily (Acts 17:11). Jesus opened the Scriptures to the Emmaus disciples by explaining them “beginning at Moses and all the prophets” (Luke 24:27).
misreadings.defence: Pentecostal scholars such as Craig Keener argue the Spirit works through careful study, not around it. Traditional evangelicals stress that the Spirit illumines what the text means; he does not add new meanings that contradict it.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Spirit and study belong together. Separating them produces either dry scholarship or unchecked private revelation.

Walk through the decision tree together with a verse that troubles someone in your group. Where did you end up?
